dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing

evidence.note: Systematically reads models.rb, lib/db.rb, job.rb, runner.rb and derives the shared job-queue BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim + status/attempts/claimed_at update semantics directly from the Ruby code — subtle cross-runtime contract nailed from source.

Plan-mode span reads all middleware (rate_limit, audit, csp, request_id) and job handlers; derives ETag (SHA256, W/"digest"), cache-control 'private, max-age=0, must-revalidate', and vary header from source — identifying subtle contracts up front (anchor-8 behavior on the reading axis).
Reads combined migrations + seed.rb + account.rb + session.rb and manually translates the 14 Sequel migrations to CREATE TABLE, mapping the schema rather than guessing.
Re-reads media.rb and corrects an assumption (blurhash is NOT generated) — source used to overturn an invented belief.
Discovers RJ_SHARED_IDS_PATH from source and re-reads runner.rb/job handlers before writing the worker — continued source grounding mid-port.

Across the entire trajectory there is NO request to the running reference server, no captured live-response fixtures, and no differential diffing — the live-probing half of the dimension is entirely absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's static source reverse-engineering is thorough and systematic — it enumerates routes, migration/job schema, header-setting middleware, and ORM/model semantics, and derives subtle contracts (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, ETag/cache-control/vary, CSP) up front, which is anchor-8-caliber on the reading axis. But it never once probes the running reference or captures live responses as ground-truth fixtures, a core requirement of both the level-5 and level-8 anchors. Excellent source derivation combined with zero live interrogation places it at 6 — clearly above anchor 5's common-case reading, but short of 8 because the empirical-oracle half is missing.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure

evidence.note: Built a working skeleton first — cargo init, main.rs /_health endpoint, start.sh, release build, and binary-size check before any feature work. Matches the 'working skeleton before feature work' part of anchor 5/8.
Entered plan mode and wrote an explicit plan file (port_rubyjournal_to_rust.md) defining project structure and subsystem ordering — genuine up-front decomposition, not just a vague todo list.

TaskCreate checkpoints mark milestone boundaries ('completed X, now doing Y') across DB→liquid→models→API→frontend→worker, showing dependency-ordered sequencing. But these are narrative 'done' claims, not concrete parity checks defining done.
The cross-runtime job queue (a named hardest piece) was implemented LAST, and feeds/FTS5 search were underdone/skipped — the opposite of anchor 8's deliberate risk-first de-risking.
Only concrete done-check observed is confirming /_health returns 200; no per-milestone parity verification, so milestones lack the concrete completion criteria anchor 8 requires.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it establishes a runnable health/build skeleton first, writes an explicit plan, and sequences subsystems by dependency with TaskCreate milestone checkpoints. But it falls short of anchor 8 because milestones are marked by narrative 'completed' statements rather than concrete per-milestone parity done-checks, and the hardest/riskiest subsystems (job queue, feeds, FTS5) were deferred to the end or skipped instead of being de-risked deliberately. This places it between the two anchors at a 6.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: All verification throughout is compilation-only ('Check compilation', 'Check compilation again', 'Build release binary'). Correctness is inferred from whether Rust code builds — never from behavioral comparison.

Prose claims it 'ensured the GET /_health endpoint returns the expected 200 OK' and 'verified the RJ_* environment variables', but there is no corresponding tool call firing an actual request; adjacent steps (192-197) are only build/binary-size checks. This is the assume-200/assume-correct pattern of anchor 0.
Zero occurrences of curl, diff, compare, parity, harness, or running the reference service. The agent never ran its own service against the live reference or diffed status/headers/JSON/HTML/feeds.
Final step is a completion claim ('implementation complete') issued during the build phase, with no differential verification stage ever reached.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's only verification signal was successful compilation, plus an unsubstantiated prose claim that /_health returns 200 — exactly the 'assumes endpoints are correct because they compile or return 200' behavior of anchor 0. There are no manual curls on real endpoints (which would reach anchor 3), no side-by-side runs of both services (anchor 5), and certainly no reusable differential harness (anchor 8). I place it at 1 rather than 0 only because of the single claimed health-endpoint check, though no request tool call backs it.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking

evidence.note: Periodic TaskCreate status notes act as a rough subsystem ledger (research→DB→Liquid→accounts→posts→frontend), showing the agent generally tracks what's done and what's next by subsystem.
Notes 'media stubs' and 'vast majority' of REST 'complete' — status is tracked by code-written, not by any parity check; stubs glossed as near-done.

Final TaskCreate declares implementation 'complete' with no differential verification ever performed — an unsubstantiated done-claim, indicating the ledger is optimistic and not reconciled against harness output.
Extended compile/type/import fix loops with no explicit recognition of thrashing or reallocation; progress-monitoring is limited to whether it compiles.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a rough, subsystem-level checklist via recurring TaskCreate status notes and generally knows what is left, which matches anchor 5's 'rough checklist.' But that ledger is tied only to code-written/compiles, never to differential-suite output (no diffs were ever run), it glosses stubs as near-complete, and ends with an unverified 'complete' claim — well short of anchor 8's harness-tied ledger and thrashing detection. This places it between the 3 and 5 anchors, at 4.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence

evidence.note: Discovers Blurhash generation isn't actually happening in the reference and updates its model ('This changes things significantly; I don't have to concern myself') — a genuine correction of a falsified assumption, but derived from reading, not from an observed diff.
Realizes shared_ids.db / RJ_SHARED_IDS_PATH matters for cross-runtime grading and adjusts shared_post_id accordingly — model update while implementing, reactive to newly-read reference detail.

Switches handler signatures from Request to HeaderMap after the extractor approach produced type errors — an implementation-approach adjustment repeated across handlers; the only design-level course change, and it's compiler-driven not reference-driven.

Long runs of compile-error patching (imports, ownership, nested Result types). Each is a real root-cause fix for the immediate error, but stays at the implementation level — no questioning of the underlying framework/library bets.

Ends declaring the port 'complete' with no differential verification against the running reference. Persistent parity diffs — the events that would falsify early bets — never surface, so no structural pivot or re-verification of a failure class ever occurs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows real but shallow course-correction: it updates its model of the reference when reading reveals wrong assumptions (Blurhash, shared_ids) and adjusts one implementation approach (Request→HeaderMap) when it fails to compile, which is above mindless symptom-patching (3). But there are no reference-driven diffs at all — the trajectory ends at 'complete' with zero differential verification — so the diff-triggered root-cause fixing of anchor 5 is only partially met, and the structural pivots/re-verification of anchor 8 (swapping a tool that can't meet a contract, confirming a class of failure is resolved) never appear. This lands between the 3 and 5 anchors, at 4.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding

evidence.note: Crate selection (rusqlite over sqlx) explicitly driven by the 40MB binary cap and compile/size impact — constraint baked into an early design decision rather than discovered late.
Measured binary size early ('8M is a great starting point') — a real proactive check, though a one-off spot check.

Deep early study of the reference job queue (job.rb, runner.rb): BEGIN IMMEDIATE, run_at/id ordering, attempts++, claimed_at — designing the cross-runtime schema/claim compat from the reference upfront.
Reaffirmed mid-work that job schema/claim/backoff/dead-letter must align precisely with reference — sustained awareness, but implemented-to-spec with no side-by-side verification under the shared DB.
Re-checked binary size on the final release build — a second constraint check, but late and not continuous.
Final verification confirms /_health returns 200 and start.sh stays foreground, but latency parity (p99 vs Ruby p50) is never measured at any point.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond a one-time check (anchor 5): binary size shaped an early crate choice and was measured twice, and the job-queue schema/claim semantics were studied deeply from the reference and designed for upfront. But it stops short of anchor 8 — it never verified job claim compatibility against the running reference under the shared DB (only implemented-to-spec), never measured latency parity at all, and treated binary size as spot checks rather than continuous monitoring. That places observed behavior at a 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity port: reimplement an entire Sinatra blog (routing, Liquid views, Sequel-shaped ORM, OAuth2, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, security headers, Markdown, FTS5 search, feeds, media, ETag caching, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue with exact BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics, admin/audit) in Rust with structural response parity against a running reference. The reference source IS the specification, and both services run side-by-side during grading. Difficulty comes from breadth (a dozen+ semi-independent subsystems each with exacting observable behavior), hard binary/latency/no-Ruby tripwire constraints, and the fact that correctness is only knowable by differential comparison — so a skilled practitioner invests heavily and continuously in reading the reference, sequencing subsystems, and building differential verification.

dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing
dimensions.description: Reading the Ruby/Sinatra reference as the executable spec and probing the running reference to nail down exact observable contracts (headers, ORM semantics, job-queue claim/backoff, migration schema, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only source of truth; every parity dimension (header sets, JSON shapes, job schema, CSP, pagination links) is undocumented except in that code and its live responses. Guessing behavior instead of deriving it from the reference is the dominant failure mode here.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from the task prose alone; never opens the reference source or hits the running reference.
anchors.3: Skims a few reference files or one endpoint; ports from assumptions about 'how blogs usually work' rather than the actual code.
anchors.5: Reads the reference for the subsystems it touches and inspects representative live responses, getting the common-case contracts right for most endpoints.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the reference before committing: enumerates routes, migration/job schema, header-setting middleware, env vars, and ORM query/ordering/soft-delete/validation semantics; captures live reference responses as ground-truth fixtures; identifies the subtle contracts (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, RFC 5988 links, CSP, conditional-GET) up front.
anchors.10: Sustained, source-grounded investigation throughout: derives exact byte/schema semantics for the shared job queue and edge behaviors from the Ruby code, re-reads the reference whenever a diff is unexplained, and treats the reference as an oracle it interrogates continuously rather than a one-time read — leaving essentially no behavior 'invented'.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into an ordered hierarchy of shippable milestones (health/skeleton first, then routing, then each subsystem) each with a concrete done-check, rather than one monolithic push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A dozen-plus subsystems with dependencies (scaffold → routing → ORM → auth → the harder feeds/search/job-queue) demand deliberate ordering; without milestones the agent cannot make or measure incremental progress across such a long horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes end-to-end with no ordering or intermediate targets.
anchors.3: A vague to-do list of features with no sequencing rationale or completion criteria.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into subsystems with rough priorities and a working skeleton before feature work.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy that sequences by dependency and risk (get /_health + build/start.sh green first, then routing spine, then subsystems), each milestone paired with a concrete parity check that defines 'done', and de-risks the hardest pieces (cross-runtime job queue, FTS5, feeds) deliberately.
anchors.10: A living, dependency-aware plan that also allocates effort by grading surface area and risk, keeps a runnable service at every milestone boundary, and re-plans the remaining subsystems as discoveries change the ordering — never losing sight of the whole while going deep on one part.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building the means to know the port is correct — firing identical requests at the Rust service and the reference and diffing status/headers/JSON/HTML/feeds/binary the way the grader does — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is defined as structural parity with a live reference; the only trustworthy signal is a diff against that reference. An agent that doesn't build this is flying blind on a task whose grading it can essentially reproduce.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints are correct because they compile or return 200.
anchors.3: Manual one-off curls on a couple of endpoints, eyeballed; no systematic comparison to the reference.
anchors.5: Runs both services and compares responses for the main endpoints, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that sends the same requests to both services and compares the way the grader will (header-set with transport noise ignored, JSON with dynamic keys elided, HTML tag-tree/text, feed UUID normalization), and runs it across subsystems to drive the work.
anchors.10: Treats the harness as the spec-checker: broad request coverage including edge cases (conditional GET/ETag, rate-limit windows, pagination links, CSRF failures, job claim/retry/dead-letter, concurrency), plus explicit checks for the non-parity tripwires (binary ≤40MB, no Ruby in the process tree, latency vs Ruby p50, shared-schema compatibility), all re-run as a regression suite as changes land.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems reach parity vs remain broken across a long horizon, and detecting when effort on one endpoint is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many subsystems and a differential suite producing lots of diffs, it is easy to lose the plot, re-fix the same thing, or believe more is done than is. An accurate done/remaining ledger is what sustains progress over this horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of overall state; no tracking of what passes or remains.
anchors.3: Occasional mental notes; frequently revisits already-'done' areas or forgets whole subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a rough checklist of subsystem status and generally knows what's left.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, updated ledger of parity status per subsystem tied to harness results, and notices when it's thrashing on one diff (repeated failed attempts) versus making progress.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise done-vs-remaining picture against differential-suite output across all subsystems, quantifies remaining risk, and explicitly recognizes stuck/circular states early and reallocates attention rather than grinding — sustaining orientation across the entire long build.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence
dimensions.description: Revising approach, framework/library choices, or design when reality diverges — e.g. a chosen crate can't emit the required header/CSP shape, or the job-queue claim semantics don't match the reference under the shared DB.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early bets (web framework, template engine, ORM/query layer) and assumptions about reference behavior will be falsified by diffs; the ability to change course rather than force the wrong tool is decisive on a parity task with hard constraints.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on falsified assumptions; ignores persistent diffs or constraint violations.
anchors.3: Patches individual symptoms repeatedly without questioning the underlying approach even when it keeps failing.
anchors.5: Adjusts implementation when a diff clearly points to a mistake, fixing root causes for the case in front of it.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a divergence is structural (a library choice, a schema/claim-semantics mismatch, a wrong model of reference behavior) and revises the design or swaps the approach, re-verifying afterward.
anchors.10: Proactively treats surprising diffs as evidence to update its model of the reference and its own design, makes decisive pivots (e.g. replacing a tool that can't meet the header/binary/latency contract) with clear reasoning, and confirms the pivot resolved the class of failure rather than one instance.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding
dimensions.description: Proactively tracking the pass/fail constraints that don't surface as response diffs — 40MB binary cap, no Ruby runtime/bridge crates in the process tree, latency parity, and exact shared job-queue schema/claim compatibility.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These constraints can silently invalidate an otherwise parity-correct port; they must be designed for from the start (crate choices affect binary size; the shared DB schema must match the reference exactly) rather than discovered at the end.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints entirely; discovers violations (oversized binary, Ruby-bridge dep, incompatible job schema) only if ever.
anchors.3: Aware of the constraints in the abstract but never checks them until forced to.
anchors.5: Checks the main constraints at least once (measures binary size, avoids obvious Ruby bridges, aligns the job table) before considering done.
anchors.8: Bakes the constraints into early decisions — chooses crates with binary size in mind, verifies the job schema/claim semantics against the reference under the shared DB, and monitors binary size and latency as work proceeds.
anchors.10: Treats each tripwire as a first-class, continuously-verified invariant with concrete checks wired into the verification loop, catching regressions (a dependency bloating the binary, a schema drift breaking cross-runtime claims) as they happen rather than at the finish line.
